lessonRef.title: Fluency and rereading practice: reading a short passage smoothly and rereading the line that slowed you down

studentTask.text: This Grade 3 lesson develops reading a short passage smoothly and rereading the line that slowed you down within the unit “Readers and Writers Begin: Habits, Print, and Sentences.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's fluency and rereading practice work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
The shelter at the corner of Nash Street had a bench, a roof, and nothing to read. Ivy noticed this on a Tuesday, while she waited eleven minutes for the number 12.

She mentioned it at dinner. Her uncle said that a person could not simply put a bookshelf at a bus stop. Rain would ruin the books. Wind would knock them over. Somebody would have to look after them.

Ivy thought about all three problems for a week. Then she asked the hardware store for a wooden crate, turned it on its side, and screwed a hinged lid across the open front. She lined the inside with a plastic bag cut flat. On the lid she painted six words: TAKE ONE. LEAVE ONE. STAY DRY.

The first day, she put in four books she had already finished twice. The second day, three of them were gone and a thin paperback about beetles had appeared. By the end of the month, the crate held books Ivy had never chosen and would never have chosen. She read the beetle book anyway. It turned out that beetles were far stranger than she expected.

Her uncle still said a person could not put a bookshelf at a bus stop. He said it, though, while returning a book to the crate.

Ivy did not argue. She had learned something better than being right: a problem with three parts can be solved three parts at a time.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “The Bus-Stop Library”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what reading a short passage smoothly and rereading the line that slowed you down asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “The Bus-Stop Library,” then answer: Choose two words or sentence parts in the reading that matter to reading a short passage smoothly and rereading the line that slowed you down. How does each part shape meaning?

Deliverable: Grade 3: a two-entry word-and-meaning annotation; write 3–5 complete sentences.

Evidence requirement: Use one exact detail. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If reading a short passage smoothly and rereading the line that slowed you down is not yet secure, return to “The Bus-Stop Library” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply reading a short passage smoothly and rereading the line that slowed you down to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “The Bus-Stop Library.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
